text.p: The dollar weakened against the German mark Wednesday after supportive comments from a German central banker encouraged investors to take profits against a recently surging British pound, foreign exchange dealers said.

Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick voiced strong doubts about the ability of weaker European countries like Italy and Spain to fix serious economic problems in time to qualify for a proposed single European currency in 1999.
The comments bolstered the mark and hurt the Italian lira, dealers said, with the mark hitting a two-week high just shy of 1000 lira.
Investors shifted funds to the mark and Japanese yen, which had fallen to attractive buying levels after a strong rally by the pound against major currencies in recent sessions, traders said.
Dealers also cited intraday drops in U.S. stock and bond prices for the dollar's decline. Demand for U.S. investments typically determines the relative demand for dollars.

"The dollar has come off its highs and I blame two things -- today's fall in U.S. asset markets and the unwinding of sterling trades," said Kevin Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank.
The dollar ended at 1.5393 marks, down from 1.5410 late Tuesday.

Against the yen, the dollar retained most of Tuesday's gains to finish little changed at 112.28 yen. The dollar failed to match Tuesday's high of 112.39, which was its highest level since January of 1994.
Koebnick said Italy and Spain will probably not be among the first nations to join Europe's planned currency union in 1999, but are likely to join by 2002.
He also said European Union members must eschew alleged budget gimmicks to meet the entry requirements for European economic and monetary union.

"All these statements saying Italy and Spain may not be able to join the union until 2002 and discussions about creative accounting have caused people to run for cover and buy marks and sell lira," said Ben Strauss, trader at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar briefly rose from early morning lows against the mark amid rumours that Russian security chief Alexander Lebed was plotting to use force to seize power, traders said.
But Lebed later denied the rumour, curtailing mark sales.

The rumour stemmed from allegations by Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikow, a key rival of Lebed, that the security chief was planning to capitalise on the health problems that have plagued Russian President Boris N. Yeltsin.
The dollar proved immune to the September consumer price index, which, as expected, showed a benign inflation picture, dealers said.
The Labour Department said consumer prices rose at a 0.3 percent pace in both the overall and the core rate, which excludes food and energy, in September.
In other trading, sterling closed at $1.5844, down from $1.5879 late Tuesday. The dollar fell to 1.2675 Swiss francs from 1.2690 and ended little changed at Canadian $1.3545.
